title: Effectiveness of Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop Generate–Validate–Repair for Natural‑Language → Configuration Translation in Emulated Multi‑Device Networks
abstract: We evaluate whether an iterative generate–validate–repair workflow that places a formal network verifier (Batfish) in the loop reduces semantic configuration errors when an LLM translates operator intents into multi‑device configuration changes. Following a preregistered paired design (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001), we sampled N=200 confirmatory multi‑device intents (stratified by topology size) and compared a single‑pass LLM generation (baseline) to a bounded verifier‑guided repair pipeline (guarded). Emulation used containerized FRRouting/VyOS images and deterministic validation rules (scorer_id deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All confirmatory pairs completed (200/200). Both baseline and guarded conditions produced 200/200 verifier‑pass outcomes (n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0), yielding an absolute paired difference = 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0) and a 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). The preregistered hypotheses are therefore not supported because the baseline already produced verifier‑passing artifacts under the controlled task‑generation and emulation regime. We incorporate preregistered artifacts and deterministic checks, provide representative intent→output examples, explicitly define the verifier‑pass decision rule used, report contamination flags (none in confirmatory N), and analyse why a ceiling effect limits exploratory inference. We conclude that, in this constrained execution regime (single model gpt‑5‑mini; FRR/VyOS emulation; deterministic synthetic intent generator), verifier‑in‑the‑loop repair did not change verifier‑measured semantic correctness; broader model and device diversity, adversarial intent sets, or higher‑fidelity device images are needed to reveal the practical marginal utility of verifier‑guided repair.

sections.introduction: Generative language models are being applied to NetOps tasks that map operator intent to device configurations. Prior work emphasizes closed‑loop validation and repair to prevent semantic outages, but the practical marginal benefit of embedding a formal verifier in an iterative generate–validate–repair loop remains unresolved. We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to answer: To what extent does an iterative generate–validate–repair loop using Batfish reduce critical semantic errors in LLM‑generated multi‑device configurations when evaluated in an emulation‑grounded closed loop? Our contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑backed confirmatory evaluation (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001) that (a) reports exact paired outcomes and statistical inference, (b) defines the verifier‑pass decision rule and contamination checks used, and (c) provides representative examples and a compact difficulty summary drawn from archived task metadata.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and benchmark papers document active work on LLMs for intent translation, agentic NetOps, and verifier‑guided pipelines [W4415071524; W4387634435; W7204209332]. Formal verification and header‑space methods (Batfish and related engines) are commonly proposed as validators for reachability and policy compliance [W4386385177]. Prior empirical work shows common failure modes (syntax errors, unsafe ordering, hallucinated commands) and motivates generate–validate–repair architectures; however, existing studies vary in task realism and model sets. Our study positions a preregistered confirmatory test within this literature by measuring the marginal effect of a bounded verifier‑guided repair loop under a controlled synthetic task generator and single LLM.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and pipeline. We preregistered CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 and froze sampling, analysis, timeouts, retry and exclusion rules (preregistration_sha256 = 163150627c4bd8d1e2520caeaa8ac0f4e0aa78876c16c3246e91596c632e49ec). Confirmatory sampling: N=200 paired intents stratified as planned into three topology clusters: (A) 2 devices: 80 intents; (B) 3–4 devices: 80 intents; (C) 5–8 devices: 40 intents. Model and generation: declared_model_version gpt‑5‑mini (provider openai_responses) with a single shared initial generation per intent; guarded condition permitted up to one verifier‑guided repair iteration. Execution: containerized emulation using FRRouting/VyOS images and Batfish as the formal verifier; deterministic scorer deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied the preregistered scoring rule “full_intent_constraint_validation” to produce a binary verifier‑pass outcome. Logging: all raw outputs, validator traces, provider traces, and contamination checks were archived and hashed (execution manifest and analysis artifacts).
sections.results: Execution and confirmatory analysis. Execution completed per plan: 400 episodes (200 baseline + 200 guarded), zero failed episodes (execution manifest completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 200). Per the archived paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv), counts were n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Baseline_success_count = 200; guarded_success_count = 200. The exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired absolute success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) estimate = 0.00 with 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00,0.00] (bootstrap_seed=1729; resamples=10000) as recorded in analysis/results.json. No repair attempts were applied for confirmatory cases because the baseline shared_initial_candidate satisfied the verifier constraints in every case (validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true and violation_count == 0 for each episode). Contamination checks: the archived contamination summary (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) contains no flags; exact SHA‑256 intent‑match count in confirmatory N = 0 and high n‑gram overlap (>80%) flags = 0 according to the archived detector outputs.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and diagnostics. The preregistered confirmatory result is a null effect caused by a ceiling: the single‑pass LLM outputs already satisfied the verifier and emulator checks under the controlled task generator and device image set. Two non‑exclusive explanations arise: (1) the specific combination of gpt‑5‑mini and the deterministic synthetic task generator produced outputs within the model's reliable generation envelope for the chosen device images; (2) the evaluation regime (task templates, FRR/VyOS images, validator expressiveness under the chosen scoring rule) did not present sufficiently challenging failure modes to require repair. Representative per‑task difficulty metadata (archived per episode) show non‑trivial task structure in the confirmatory set: in the six representative tasks provided in the archived manifest, changed_interface_count across examples = {1,2,2,2,2,2} (mean = 1.83, median = 2), required_command_count = {4,2,6,4,3,6} (mean = 4.17, median = 4), dependency_rule_count ∈ {1,2,2,2,2,2}, and level labels include medium/hard/very_hard. These representative figures demonstrate that tasks required multi‑step, dependency‑sensitive sequences (e.g., make‑before‑break or shutdown→configure→restore patterns). Nevertheless, because no confirmatory episode produced a verifier failure, planned secondary and exploratory analyses (iterations‑to‑pass curves, topology dependence) are vacuous for the confirmatory cohort and are therefore limited to the archived exploratory reserve. Statistical note on degeneracy. When a paired test yields zero discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0), the McNemar statistic is degenerate; exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap of the paired difference under the observed contingency produces a point estimate and CI of exactly zero. Our analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) record these values and the bootstrap parameters (seed=1729, resamples=10000). Operational implication. This null confirmatory outcome does not imply that verifier‑in‑the‑loop architectures are unnecessary in practice; rather it highlights that task selection, model diversity, emulator fidelity, and adversarial intent distributions are critical to evaluating the marginal utility of verifier‑guided repair.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired confirmatory evaluation of a bounded verifier‑in‑the‑loop generate–validate–repair pipeline versus single‑pass LLM generation for NL→config translation in emulated multi‑device networks. Under the constrained conditions studied (gpt‑5‑mini, FRR/VyOS emulation, deterministic synthetic task generator), baseline single‑pass outputs passed the formal verifier for all confirmatory tasks, producing a null marginal effect for the guarded repair stage (paired difference 0.00; McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]). We provide deterministic execution artifacts, representative examples, contamination checks (none flagged), and explicit scoring semantics. Future experiments should broaden model and device diversity, incorporate vendor‑specific images and operator‑authored intents, and include adversarial and noisy intent sets to expose realistic failure modes where verifier‑guided repair would be beneficial.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory). This study was executed autonomously from a frozen initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). LLM used: declared_model_version gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). Orchestration / adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 was frozen before execution (preregistration_sha256 = 163150627c4bd8d1e2520caeaa8ac0f4e0aa78876c16c3246e91596c632e49ec) and bound sampling, analysis, retry, timeout, and inclusion/exclusion rules. Execution components used: containerized Mininet‑style emulation with FRRouting and VyOS images, Batfish as the formal verifier, deterministic task generator, and the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scoring rule (scorer applied the archived validator_trace fields to decide verifier_pass). All experimental design, generation, model calls, verification, emulation runs, scoring, hashing, logging, and analysis were performed autonomously per the execution manifest. The archived execution manifest, raw responses, validator traces, analysis artifacts (including paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, analysis/contamination_summary.csv), and the preregistration manifest are provided in the artifact bundle for machine verification. Humans acted only as Research Director prior to the autonomy lock and to receive final outputs after autonomous completion; no human manually edited manuscript technical content, results, analysis, references, figures, captions, or this Disclosure Statement after the autonomy lock. Execution completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs (execution manifest failed_episode_count = 0).
limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across models or vendors.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images).
Synthetic task generator: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture the full ambiguity, diversity, or adversarial distribution of real operator intents or legacy runbooks.
Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully replicate hardware idiosyncrasies or timing/race conditions of production devices.
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the verifier for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting exploratory inferences.

Contamination risk: deterministic exact‑hash checks found zero exact matches in confirmatory N and archived n‑gram overlap detectors reported zero high‑overlap flags, but undetected paraphrase overlap with LLM training data cannot be fully ruled out.
Security scenarios: prompt‑injection, retrieval poisoning, and adversarial telemetry perturbations were not evaluated and remain open threats for agentic NetOps systems.
